status: Five full-text sources are recorded with bounded locators and per-result dispositions; Wainwright–Jordan and Geyer are independent exponential-family treatments, with the full Geyer lecture notes serving as the required primary course treatment.

sources.title: Martin J. Wainwright and Michael I. Jordan, Graphical Models, Exponential Families, and Variational Inference, Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 1(1–2) (2008)
sources.locator: §3.2; §3.5.1 Proposition 2; §3.5.2 Propositions 3 and Theorem 1 with Appendix B.1 proof; §3.6; and §6.1, printed pp. 38–40, 61–65, 146–147, 257–258 / PDF pp. 44–46, 67–71, 152–153, 263–264.

contents.name: §3.5.1 Derivatives and convexity, Proposition 2
contents.support: The source differentiates the log partition function to obtain the mean and covariance and identifies strict convexity under minimality. The local statement fixes finite full support and the proof checks the inherited envelope hypothesis before using the covariance identity.

contents.name: §3.5.2 Forward mapping to mean parameters, Proposition 3
contents.support: The source states injectivity of the gradient map exactly for minimal representations. The local proof separately checks equality and noninjectivity of the probability family itself.

contents.name: §3.5.2 Theorem 1 and Appendix B.1 proof of the gradient map range
contents.support: The source proves that mean parameters in the interior are attained in minimal families. The local proof supplies the finite-support coercivity and boundary nonattainment argument needed for the exact iff statement.

contents.name: §6.1 Estimation in fully observed models
contents.support: The source writes the IID exponential-family log likelihood as the empirical-statistic mean paired with the canonical parameter minus the log partition function, and records moment matching when the empirical mean is interior. The local proof also establishes nonexistence at every support-boundary sample.

contents.name: §3.2 Basics of exponential families
contents.support: Defines the canonical family using sufficient statistics and the log partition function relative to a base measure. The local item specializes to finite positive weights and proves normalization and the compact-envelope regularity needed for derivative identities.

contents.name: §3.5.2 Theorem 1 and Appendix B.1 supporting geometry
contents.support: Provides the convex-support/interior route associated with the gradient-map range. The local finite-supporting-direction lemma is proved independently by compact projection, rational approximation, and a convergent unit-normal subsequence.

contents.name: §3.6 conjugate dual and empirical log likelihood
contents.support: Relates the conjugate optimization to the rescaled empirical log likelihood and the interior mean-parameter case. The local theorem proves existence by coercivity and proves boundary nonexistence by a supporting direction.

contents.name: §6.2.1 Exact EM algorithm in exponential families
contents.support: Treats observed and latent variables through a joint exponential-family model and its conditional latent law. The local definition allows a general parameter-measurable observation kernel and proves its finite-state marginalization directly; no EM or exactness result is imported.

sources.title: Charles J. Geyer, Stat 8931 (Exponential Families) Lecture Notes: Two Examples of Agresti (2016)
sources.locator: §2 Introduction, §3.2 Calculating the Linearity, and §4.6.3 Return to Confidence Regions, printed pp. 1–2, 8–9, 55–56 / PDF pp. 0–1, 8–9, 56–57.

contents.name: §2 Introduction: boundary means and canonical MLEs at infinity
contents.support: The notes explain with finite exponential-family examples that an observed mean on the relative boundary can yield no finite canonical parameter. The B-page example computes the two-state case directly.

contents.name: §3.2 Calculating the Linearity: existence criterion via tangent-cone linearity
contents.reason: The general tangent-cone algorithm and its criterion cite a separate 2009 theorem and are not needed for the finite IID proof; the assigned finite boundary case is proved directly from a supporting direction.

contents.name: §4.6.3 Return to Confidence Regions: relative interiors of convex-support faces
contents.support: The notes locate an MLE in the relative interior of the face supporting the observed statistic. In the local minimal finite case the convex support is full-dimensional, so its relative interior is its ordinary interior.

contents.name: §2 full-support canonical exponential-family examples
contents.support: Supplies canonical finite-family examples and the boundary-MLE contrast. The local definition proves its finite normalization for arbitrary positive reference weights.

contents.name: §4.6.3 relative interiors of convex-support faces
contents.support: Provides context for relative-interior geometry of finite convex supports; the local supporting-direction claim and all its hypotheses are proved directly.

sources.title: Julian Besag, Statistical Analysis of Non-Lattice Data, The Statistician 24(3) (1975), pp. 179–195
sources.locator: §1, printed pp. 179–181, for conditional distributions and local neighborhoods; §3.3, printed pp. 190–192, especially equation (3.2) and its true-likelihood qualification. Full scanned PDF retrieved and relevant pages inspected by rendering.

contents.name: §1 Introduction: conditioning one site on the remaining sites and defining local neighbors
contents.support: The paper defines site-conditional distributions and explains that a local neighborhood is the set of sites on which a conditional depends. The local definition makes the finite-volume region, fixed exterior boundary, interaction collection, and each finite neighborhood explicit.

contents.name: §3.3 A Pseudo-likelihood Technique, equation (3.2)
contents.support: The paper defines the pseudo log likelihood as the sum of log one-site conditional probabilities and explicitly distinguishes it from the true sample log likelihood except under independence. The B-page two-spin computation verifies a concrete posterior consequence.

contents.name: §3.3 consistency discussion and its infinite-volume regularity conditions
contents.reason: No spatial asymptotic consistency claim is made here; that route requires a separate identifiability and mixing or ergodic theorem, including boundary control.

contents.name: §3.3 equation (3.2), pseudo-likelihood versus joint likelihood
contents.support: Distinguishes the product of site-conditional probabilities from the joint likelihood. The local two-spin calculation derives the exact and pseudo-posterior odds and shows they differ.

sources.title: Alicia A. Johnson, Miles Q. Ott, and Mine Dogucu, Bayes Rules!, Chapter 2: Bayes’ Rule
sources.locator: §§2.1.1–2.1.2, 2.3.5–2.4: proper prior model, data-conditional likelihood, marginal normalizer, normalized posterior rule, and chapter summary.

contents.name: §2.1.1 Prior probability model
contents.support: The chapter treats a prior as a probability model for the parameter. The local definition requires a proper prior and separately defines the observation kernel.

contents.name: §2.1.2 Conditional probability and likelihood
contents.support: The chapter distinguishes a data-conditional sampling law from the likelihood function at an observed datum. The local density branch defines a common dominating measure and sums the hidden Gibbs configurations before likelihood evaluation.

contents.name: §2.3.5 Posterior probability model and equations (2.10)–(2.13)
contents.support: The chapter derives the posterior as prior times likelihood divided by the marginal normalizer in a finite probability model. The local theorem proves the dominated-kernel formula by Tonelli and relies on a separate standard-Borel supplier for the general posterior kernel.

contents.name: §2.4 Chapter summary: prior, sampling model, likelihood, posterior
contents.support: The four components are reflected in the local prior, latent Gibbs law, marginal sampling kernel, and posterior construction.

sources.title: Hugo Touchette, The Large Deviation Approach to Statistical Mechanics (2009)
sources.locator: Historical bounded reading recorded in research/frontier-expansion-2026-10-19/classical-statistical-mechanics/sources.md: PDF p. 19 and pp. 24–26 on the Varadhan principle and finite empirical measures/cumulant limitations.

contents.name: Varadhan principle and finite empirical-measure limits
contents.reason: This inverse-Gibbs pair makes no large-deviation, posterior-concentration, or asymptotic cumulant claim; the related results remain on the required large-deviation prerequisite page.
